summary: This document extends BGP route reflectors so they choose the best route from the viewpoint of their clients instead of their own, using IGP cost from configured locations. It can be per client, per group or for all clients, and helps deployments with centralized route reflectors that want hot potato routing.

eli5.summary: A middle manager normally picks what is best from their own desk. This document makes the manager pick what is best from the worker's desk instead.

questions: what is bgp optimal route reflection
why does a route reflector pick the wrong exit
what is an igp location in bgp orr
subtitle: Lets a BGP route reflector pick exits from its clients' point of view instead of its own.

tldr.problem: A route reflector normally picks the exit point closest to itself and passes only that best path to its clients, which sit elsewhere in the network. When reflectors are placed outside the forwarding path, the clients get exits that are not the best for them, which defeats hot potato routing.
tldr.mechanism: The operator configures an IGP location, a node in the IGP topology, and the reflector computes the interior cost to each BGP next hop from that location. The reflector can run more than one Decision Process, one per client, per set of clients, or for all clients.
tldr.outcome: Clients get the path they would have chosen themselves from the same candidate paths, and the clients need no changes. It relies on all route reflectors learning all eligible paths, which needs BGP ADD-PATH between reflectors.

facts.label: IGP location
facts.value: A node, identified by an IP address such as a loopback

facts.label: Granularity
facts.value: Per route reflector, per set of clients, or per client

today: RFC 9107 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Route Reflectors Pick Poorly
sections.content:
Within one Autonomous System, route reflection (RFC 4456) is described as the most popular way to distribute BGP routes between BGP speakers. The catch is that IGP cost to a given point varies from router to router, so route reflection may not give the same result as a full IBGP mesh.

That hurts hot potato routing, which sends traffic to the closest exit point of the AS when no higher-priority policy says otherwise. The exit a reflector picks is the one best for the reflector, not necessarily for its clients.

The problem grows when reflectors sit outside the forwarding path, often in arbitrary places in the core. A reflector that knows several paths for a route usually advertises only its best one. If an IGP tie-break chose it, that path is the exit closest to the reflector, and the clients are somewhere else in the topology.
sections.eli5: Imagine a teacher choosing the closest door out of the school for the whole class, but from the teacher's own spot. The door that is closest to the teacher may be far from the kids at the back.

sections.title: The Core Idea: An IGP Location
sections.content:
The operator specifies an IGP location for which the reflector calculates interior cost to the next hop. It is a node in the IGP topology, identified by an IP address of that node such as a loopback address. It can be set per route reflector, per set of clients, or per client.

The reflector then selects and distributes routes with the shortest distance to the next hops from the selected location. This frees the reflector from its physical location and allows transient or permanent migration of this control-plane function to an arbitrary location with no impact on IP transit.

An implementation is compliant if it supports at least one of these grouping categories. A client can differ from the reflector in two ways: it has a different position in the IGP topology, and it can have a different routing policy. A significant advantage is that the clients do not need to be modified.
sections.eli5: Instead of choosing a door from where the teacher stands, the teacher picks a spot in the hallway where the kids actually are, and measures distances from there.

sections.title: Changing the Tie-Break Step
sections.content:
The change targets step e) of Section 9.1.2.2 ("Breaking Ties (Phase 2)") of RFC 4271. The old text computes the interior cost using the metric to the NEXT_HOP via the Routing Table. The new text computes the metric from the selected IGP location to the NEXT_HOP, using the shortest IGP path tree rooted at that location. Other policy steps are not affected.

To compute that tree the reflector needs the IGP topology of the area or level containing each location. It can learn it from a link-state IGP such as IS-IS or OSPF, or via BGP-LS (RFC 7752). When a location is given for a group of clients, one or more backup IGP locations SHOULD be allowed for redundancy.

If the BGP next hop is itself a BGP route, the IGP metric used for its resolution SHOULD be the final IGP cost to reach it. An implementation that cannot tell BGP that final metric MUST treat such paths as least preferred in next-hop metric comparisons, but MUST still consider them valid for Phase 2 selection.
sections.eli5: Where the old rule measured distance from the reflector, the new rule measures it from the chosen spot. If the spot disappears, a backup spot takes over.

sections.title: Running Several Decision Processes
sections.content:
A standard reflector runs one BGP Decision Process. BGP ORR may need several Decision Processes, or subsets of one, to cover different IGP locations or policies for different sets of clients. The RFC says this is very similar to what RFC 7947 defines for route servers.

If only the IGP cost to the next hop differs, only step e) and the later steps need to run multiple times. If different clients need different BGP policies, for example for traffic engineering or dedicated exit points, a larger part of the process must repeat, up to the whole Decision Process of Section 9.1 of RFC 4271. A general policy can first be applied for a set of clients, and regular selection with the client's IGP perspective is then applied to the remaining candidates.
sections.eli5: Instead of making one decision for everybody, the reflector makes a separate decision for each group, using that group's own spot and rules.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Optimal routing between clients of different clusters relies on all route reflectors learning all eligible paths, so BGP ADD-PATH (RFC 7911) needs to be deployed between reflectors. The solution works with hop-by-hop forwarding and with end-to-end tunnels, but to avoid loops without encapsulation the reflection topology must be designed carefully (see Section 11 of RFC 4456).

If a backup IGP location is configured, it is used when the primary location disappears from the IGP. As with a reflector failure, the paths may change and are generally expected to be less optimal; the smaller the distance between primary and backup locations, the smaller the impact.

Precision costs computing power, since each IGP location needs its own SPF calculation and Decision Process. An IGP location per client gives the highest precision, per set of clients less, and one for the whole instance the lowest, equal to RFC 4456 reflection. Compared with ADD-PATH on all routers, BGP ORR reduces the state pushed to the network edge.
sections.eli5: The more separate decisions you make, the more work the reflector has to do. You choose between very exact answers for each kid and cheaper answers for whole groups.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The extension provides a new metric value using additional information for computing routes. The RFC notes that any improperly used metric value could affect network resiliency, but this extension does not change the underlying security issues of IBGP as described in RFC 4456, and it introduces no requirements for new protection measures. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: It does not add new doors for troublemakers. The safety rules stay the same as before, and nothing new has to be registered anywhere.
